We are excited to announce Leanstral 1.5, Mistral’s most capable open weight Lean model brought to you by @Aditi Kabra, @Albert Jiang, Andrew Zhao, @Dhia Garbaya , @Indraneel Mukherjee, @Jason Rute, @Mert Ünsal, @Roman Soletskyi, and @Simon Sorg. It saturates miniF2F, solves 587/672 PutnamBench problems, and achieves 34% on FATE-X and 43.2% on FLTEval. Moreover, it is open source and a fraction of size and cost of other models.

We are offering Leanstral 1.5 for free through API and Mistral Vibe and strongly encourage everyone here to give it a try. If you are familiar with code agents like Claude Code or Codex, it will be a very familiar experience. We found it to be a very capable model for Lean coding. Post your impressions here!

Installing Mistral Vibe and Leanstral

  • If you have already installed Leanstral it should automatically use the new model.
  • Verify your Mistral account settings at https://admin.mistral.ai/
    • Sign up or Sign in
    • You can stay on the free plan (there is no need to sign up to Mistral Pro to use Leanstral).
    • Opt into “Enable Labs models” in https://admin.mistral.ai/plateforme/privacy
    • Make an API key in https://admin.mistral.ai/organization/api-keys
  • Follow the instructions to install the mistral vibe CLI at https://docs.mistral.ai/getting-started/quickstarts/vibe-code/install-cli
    • Setup should happen automatically, requesting your API key. But if not, use vibe --setup from the terminal.
    • If you get an error about not being able to open a browser, type m to manually enter your API key.
  • To setup Leanstral in Mistral vibe enter:
    • /leanstall (lean + [in]stall)
    • exit (to leave vibe)

Using Leanstral

  • Type vibe --agent lean in the terminal (ensure Leanstral displays at the top).
    • We recommend running vibe inside vs code terminal so you can see both vibe and your code.
    • We recommend running vibe inside your Lean project directory.
    • To auto-approve model changes (be careful!), use vibe --agent lean --yolo.
  • Ask Leanstral to do any coding task for you, such as prove a given theorem or fix some code in your project.
  • Leanstral is capable of doing very long range tasks which requires hours of work. Don’t hesitate to let it work away at a problem.

Install Lean LSP MCP (Optional)

It is highly recommended to install Lean LSP MCP by adding the following to your ~/.vibe/config.toml

[[mcp_servers]]
name = "lean-lsp"
transport = "stdio"
command = "uvx"
args = ["lean-lsp-mcp"]
tool_timeout_sec = 600

If there are no existing MCP servers, you may have to remove mcp_servers = [].

Paper: https://github.com/mistralai/LeanstralSafeVerify/blob/main/LeanstralReport.pdf

Blog Post: https://mistral.ai/news/leanstral-1-5/

Model: https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Leanstral-1.5-119B-A6B

I find Leanstral 1.5 to be able to grind for many many hours on end, so I always use --yolo to let to work on a task without me supervising and it's quite a nice experience, but you are at your own risk with --yolo :)

Model is much smaller than Opus/GPT 5.5 (limited compute :grimacing:) so it may require more handholding - but once you have a sorry, just ask it to prove it and let it run!

Would be really interesting for us to see where it shines for all folks here and where it comes short

Can you explain how you choose which provers to compare against? E.g. the current number 1 at https://lean-lang.org/eval/ is Aristotle but it's not used in the comparison despite arguably being one of the systems that the community deploys frequently in practice. Similarly for less specialized systems like Claude or Codex. I think comparing against the systems that are most frequently used in the community might make sense to help people estimate better which systems they should look into or if the common AI benchmarks reflect ability of these systems in their day to day work (if e.g. the leaders in these benchmarks are not actually helpful at the tasks agents are used for by the community it would seem to me that the benchmarks might measure the wrong thing?)

Relatedly I was also wondering if you are planning on giving leanstral 1.5 a run on lean-eval? The previous leanstral release sits quite low on the leaderboard and it would be cool to see an open source model climb the ranks.a

Hi Henrik, please see section 3.1.5 of our tech report https://github.com/mistralai/LeanstralSafeVerify/blob/main/LeanstralReport.pdf on lean eval. The TLDR is that lean-eval is very much a benchmark in progress and people submit solutions as new problems come out. I'm sure Kim will agree with this. Therefore you really really shouldn't use it to compare models!

We do plan to give it a go once Kim finalises a version 1.0 or 0.1 for lean-eval!

For putnambench, we go by the leaderboard: https://trishullab.github.io/PutnamBench/leaderboard.html.
For FATE, we go by self-reported scores.
miniF2F almost everyone solves it.
FLTEval we just released. We will bench all the latest models as soon as we fix the definition ambiguity issue as we explained in the tech report.

Full disclaimer: I once ran Leanstral on a very early version of lean-eval when there were only small number of problems and in some problems model exhibits what we call "laziness" where it claims task is too difficult and requires adding a lot of new things to Mathlib. This happens in particular when the given problem is some research-level mathematics (happened when I asked it to formalize unit-distance result). With that being said, if you decompose a little bit and ask it to do some sublemmas it will attack them!

Sure I do agree you shouldn't use lean-eval as a benchmark in your tech report, I was more using it to justify that it looks like some provers such as Aristotle seem to be both very capable (also compared to models that you do compare against like the mentioned SeedProver though not by a lot) and used by the community. So they might make for an interesting comparison target. But good to hear that you do plan on extending the eval on your own dataset!

In general I do wonder whether the reason that Aristotle and general purpose LLMs seem to be the dominant ones in the community (at least judging from the amount of mentions they receive outside of the AI research channels compared to systems like Leanstral, Seed Prover etc.) is purely a social effect (i.e. the other systems are capable but not used much for non-technical reasons like UX, availability, marketing etc.) or whether it is because what the benchmarks measure is not actually what the community is using the models for (in which case it seems like we need different benchmarks)

First impression (of letting it loose on a file with some sorry'd theorems inside a Docker container and repository with some custom definitions and theorems in several files):

Leanstral solved some (easier) theorems, fixed a broken pre-existing proof, and since then has been working on a different harder theorem, where it regularly decides to "start over", using git to reset the file to the original state, thereby losing work on theorems which it already had proven (unless it saved progress in a way that I can't see, which would have to be outside the repository).

Huggingface quants containing Q4_K_M weights (and more coming) for the very small set of people on this Zulip who wish to run models locally. Q4_K_M at 67.2GB. I'm running it locally at 325 t/s prompt processing, 48.43 t/s generation, quite usable!

Congrats on the release! Running it on some open-source project. Long-running tasks was a particular pain point for me using the original Leanstral.

My task for Leanstral is to do a (potentially very large) refactor of Lean project translated from Rocq to remove the Rocq-ness (e.g. Unit all over the place, using xxx = true instead of Prop sprinkled with Decidable). I think Leanstral might not be intended to be run as a high-level planning agent. The pain points I encountered are:

  1. It's not so good at using bash and other simple tools when researching context and planning. For example, instead of using the edit tool, for large edits it would often cp plan.md /dev/null and then cat plan.md << EOF the new plan. I don't really trust LLMs to copy content verbatim. In many cases, changes are easy to check via git diff so probably not a big deal.
  2. Its investigations are often quite shallow. For example, in the refactoring task above, it looks at the top-level, "big boss" theorem and sees def isComplete (_ : Unit) : Bool = branch1 && branch2 && branch3, and decides to just modify isComplete to a Prop and without digging down to branch1, branch2, etc. I did miss it in the initial instructions, but I have to nudge it two times until it truly digs deep. Compared to Opus, without any prompting, it asks me whether I want to just fix the shallow surface APIs or dig deep and completely eliminate the pattern.

Through the refactoring task, I found that the model is quite good at filling in sorrys that don't need helper lemmas, but it seems like it doesn't have the high-level understanding/intelligence that SOTA models do for large-scale foundational refactoring that would ripple across the codebase, probably as expected. I don't want this to come across as a criticism, because the fact that we're seriously comparing an open-source, 200B model with something SOTA like Fable is already unthinkable. There's just no parallel universe where this would go up against Opus/Fable in terms of intelligence, so some creative model collaboration is probably needed to extract the best value out of it.

Admittedly I've yet to give it a complex program-verification proof (e.g. Fable produced a 2K line proof) with a sorry and just let it go wild. I have some coming up this week, and will give it a try!

I would imagine there is a great use case of using SOTA as the high-level planning and strategy and Leanstral for quick, rapid execution. Fable/Opus 4.8, even though gets stuff correct a lot, are super slow, and maybe by combining the advantages of both we can get the best of both worlds.

It has been extremely difficult to squeeze in both good coding abilities as well as formal performance into a 120B model. We have made a choice to prioritize formal, particularly, the task of filling sorries and autoformalization. I agree that as a general coding companion, the model is worse than Opus/Fable/GPT 5.5 which are probably trained with at least x100 more compute.

My hope is that this model can be used as a cheap/fast agent that can reliably complete concrete tasks. In particular, this could work great in automated multi-agent setups (e.g. Opus as orchestrator and Leanstral as subagent)!
